opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question. If I could go back and talk to my first-year PhD self, I think the first thing I'd say is: don't be afraid to work on something that feels a little unusual, as long as you genuinely care about it. When I started, there was this pressure to pick whatever topic was hot at the moment, because that's where the papers and the citations seemed to be. But the projects that ended up mattering most to me were the ones where I was solving a problem I personally ran into and felt frustrated by. That frustration is actually a really good signal. If something annoys you enough, chances are it annoys other people too, and you have the motivation to push through the hard parts.

The second thing is about depth versus breadth. Early on, I'd tell myself to go deep on one thing first. Build real expertise, understand the fundamentals, whether that's the math, the systems, or the hardware underneath. It's tempting to skim many areas, but genuine contributions usually come from knowing something better than almost anyone else, and then later connecting it to other fields. A lot of interesting ideas come from those intersections, like bringing compiler techniques into physical simulation, but you can only make those connections if you really understand at least one side deeply.

Third, I'd say: build things people can actually use. A paper is great, but if you can turn your research into a tool, open-source it, and let others build on it, the impact multiplies in a way you can't predict. Users will find applications you never imagined, and their feedback makes your research better. It's more work, of course, writing documentation, fixing bugs, answering questions, but I think it's absolutely worth it.

And finally, take care of yourself and be patient. A PhD is a marathon. There will be months where nothing works, where your experiments fail and reviewers reject your papers. That's normal. It doesn't mean you're not good enough. What matters is that you keep learning and keep moving forward. So, pick problems you love, go deep, make your work useful to others, and don't burn out along the way. That's what I'd tell myself.

r001.rationale: The response recommends choosing personally meaningful problems and building deep expertise, but does not advise deciding what research is important before committing time to executing a research plan.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The first thing I'd tell my first-year self is: stop trying to pick the perfect problem before you start. I spent too long agonizing over whether a direction was "important enough," when the honest truth is you can't judge that from the outside. You learn what a problem really is by getting your hands dirty, building something, breaking it, and seeing where the friction shows up. The good problems announce themselves once you're close enough to notice them.

The second thing is to build tools, not just papers. When I started working on physical simulation, a huge amount of my time went into writing and rewriting the same low-level code, fighting the compiler, fighting the GPU. At some point I realized that the bottleneck wasn't my ideas, it was the infrastructure. That frustration eventually became Taichi. In hindsight, the "boring" engineering problems that slow you down every day are often the most valuable ones to solve, because if they're slowing you down, they're slowing everyone down. A good tool compounds. A single paper usually doesn't.

Third, optimize for learning rate, not for early results. In your first year it's tempting to chase a quick publication to feel legitimate. But the skills that actually matter later, writing clearly, knowing the systems stack deeply, understanding the math well enough to explain it to a freshman, those take a long time to build and nobody will push you to build them. Pick projects that force you to grow, even if they're slower.

And finally, talk to people more. I was quite shy and assumed everyone else knew what they were doing. They didn't. Some of my best directions came from a hallway conversation where someone said, "that's annoying, why hasn't anyone fixed it?" Research is much less lonely and much more fun when you treat it as a collaborative sport.

So, in short: start building before you feel ready, take the tooling problems seriously, invest in skills over quick wins, and keep talking to people.

r001.rationale: The response advises starting hands-on before deciding whether a problem is important, rather than assessing importance before committing to a research plan.

astra-6.text:
I’d tell myself to spend more time choosing the problem before rushing into solving it. When you start a PhD, it’s tempting to pick something because it looks technically difficult or because it seems likely to become a paper. But you also want to ask: If this works, why will it matter? Who will care about the result?

Then I’d say, build something small and test your assumptions early. You can spend months making an idea more sophisticated without checking whether the basic idea is useful. A simple prototype can teach you a lot.

And be persistent about the question, but flexible about the approach. If an approach doesn’t work, that’s information. You don’t have to defend it just because you’ve invested time in it. The goal is to learn something meaningful, not to prove that your first idea was right.

r001.rationale: The response advises choosing the research problem and asking why it matters before rushing into solving it.

sol-6.1.text:
I would tell myself to spend more time figuring out which problems I really care about. Early in a PhD, it’s easy to look at what other people are publishing and think, “Okay, I should work on that too.” But you want a question that you’ll still be curious about when the experiments don’t work and nobody else is paying attention.

Then, once you have a direction, make something concrete as quickly as possible. Build a small prototype, test the key assumption, and let the results change your mind. You don’t need to commit to the whole thesis on day one. You need a useful next experiment.

And I’d encourage myself to talk to people earlier. Don’t wait until an idea feels polished. A conversation can expose a bad assumption or help you see a much more interesting question. Be patient with the big problem, but move quickly on learning whether your approach makes sense.

r001.rationale: The candidate advises first identifying which research problems they genuinely care about, then choosing a direction and beginning concrete work.
